description.summary: Vitrin OS wire protocol v0 (wire version integer 1)

protocol.description:
The single IDL source of truth for the Vitrin OS wire protocol: the principal-facing interfaces spoken by agent clients over the core's listening socket, and the shim-facing interfaces spoken by per-app shims over a core-inherited socketpair. Both connection classes share one wire format; they differ only in authentication and dispatch table.
CONNECTION CLASSES. The class of a connection is fixed at accept time by the transport, never negotiated on the wire: connections on the listening socket ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/vitrin-0/core.sock) are principal connections; connections on a core-inherited socketpair are shim connections. Object 1 on a principal connection is vitrin_handshake; object 1 on a shim connection is vitrin_shim_session. Neither class's interfaces are reachable from the other: a message using the other class's opcodes dies as a fatal protocol error with no special casing.
FRAMING. Little-endian on the wire. Each message is one frame with an 8-byte header: object_id (u32), size (u16, whole frame including header; a declared size below the 8-byte header minimum, or a payload shorter than the size declares, is fatal "oversized" - and because the field is u16 the 65535-byte ceiling binds senders, which MUST NOT construct a larger frame, rather than receivers, which cannot observe one), opcode (u8), fd_count (u8, 0 or 1 - at most one file descriptor per message is a framing invariant; because the count is in the header, a receiver can drop any frame and still consume and close its fd without consulting the schema). Argument types form a closed set of seven: int (s32), uint (u32), fixed (signed 24.8), string, object (u32 id), new_id (u32 id), fd (SCM_RIGHTS, matched positionally). Strings are a u32 byte length followed by UTF-8 (no NUL terminator on the wire, embedded NUL forbidden), padded to 4 bytes; each string argument documents a maximum byte length, and violations are fatal "invalid_argument". There are no arrays and no 64-bit scalars in version 1.
OBJECT IDS. Object ids are per-connection u32 values. 0 is the null object (legal only for arguments marked allow-null); 1 is the bootstrap object, implicit at connect and never created by a message. Client- allocated ids MUST be strictly increasing and are never reused, in the range [2, 0xfeffffff]; the range [0xff000000, 0xffffffff] is reserved to the server and unused in version 1 (no event carries a new_id, so the server never allocates). When one request carries several new_id arguments, they MUST be distinct, strictly increasing in argument order, and all above the connection's allocation watermark; any violation is fatal "invalid_object". Version 1 defines no destructors: objects live for the connection, and objects derived from a grant become inert when the grant dies (requests on them are refused recoverably, never fatally). The server MAY emit events that reference an object whose grant has died; clients MUST tolerate and discard such events - this is safe forever because ids are never reused.
ORDERING. Each direction of a connection is a single ordered stream: the server processes requests in order, the client receives events in order, and ordering holds across objects within the connection. This guarantee is load-bearing: it is what makes the sync barrier, the buffer_done cookie protocol, pipelined capture pairing, and a threadless blocking client SDK correct with no additional machinery.
ERROR TAXONOMY. A failure is FATAL (the connection dies) when the client violated something it could have known - the grammar, the handshake order, or its own connection's object graph - or breached a documented per-connection resource bound (the petition-rate ceiling, the live-object cap, or id exhaustion: fatal "resource_exhausted", a denial-of-service confinement, not a semantic judgement). A failure is RECOVERABLE (an event is delivered and the connection lives) when a well-formed request's authority or target changed underneath it: consent outcome, expiry, revocation, human preemption, a granted verb's rate ceiling, or shim death. Corollary: once a grant is revoked or expired its objects go inert - requests on them yield recoverable refusals, never "invalid_object" death - otherwise human revocation racing in-flight requests would kill well-behaved agents. Fatal errors on principal connections are carried by vitrin_handshake.error and then the connection closes; shim connections carry no fatal-error message (a shim protocol violation is log-and-close: the shim is a core-spawned disposable child, and the core log is the debugging channel).
DELIVERY CLASSIFICATION. Requests are classified reply-bearing (hello, sync, request_grant, capture_frame), fire-and-forget (move, button, scroll, type, attach, damage, commit), or structural mints (get_realm, create_surface, get_seat), which are neither reply-bearing nor refusable: the request only mints an object, with no terminal event and no wire acknowledgement - a malformed mint is a fatal object-graph error, and a mint whose target is unknown or vacant surfaces that on first use, never at mint time. Every reply-bearing request receives exactly one terminal event, in request order (petition resolution excepted - see PETITION EVENT ORDERING), and such terminals are never coalesced. Refusals of fire-and-forget requests MAY be coalesced: at most one refused(rate_limited) per grant per bucket-refill window, and at most one refused per grant per (verb, code) pair until a subsequent request on that grant succeeds. The sync barrier bounds refusal discovery to one round trip.
VERSIONING. The protocol version is a single integer: the version attribute of this document and the first argument of hello. The v0 in the document family's name (vitrin-v0.xml) is the spec generation; the wire integer it carries starts at 1 (the schema forbids 0). Prose that says "version 1" means this wire integer. Version 1 requires an exact match; a mismatch is fatal "version_unsupported" (downgrade is refusal, not negotiation). Growth is Wayland-style: new messages are appended with since attributes (opcodes are implicit document order, requests and events numbered separately from 0), enum entries are appended (values are immutable; deprecated-since marks, never removes), and a message signature is immutable forever - extension is a new message, never a changed one.
ENUM AND BITFIELD VALIDATION. An enum-referencing argument is strictly validated. A plain enum argument is checked by whole-value membership: a value that is not a defined entry is fatal "invalid_argument". A bitfield="true" enum argument is checked as a bitmask: any bit set outside the union of defined entry values is out-of-range and fatal "invalid_argument", while any combination of defined bits is legal. Thus request_grant's verbs accepts observe|actuate_pointer|actuate_text (value 7) but a bit reserved for a future verb (for example value 8) is fatal. This is distinct from a policy refusal: outcome "unsupported" concerns a well-formed, in-range request the deployment declines to serve, never an out-of-range wire value.
ENUM REFERENCES. An enum attribute names the enum a scalar argument draws from. A bare name (for example "origin") refers to an enum defined on the argument's own interface; a dotted name (for example "vitrin_view.format") refers to an enum on the named interface. The code generator resolves references by this rule to build membership and mask tables.
STRING BOUNDS. Every string argument declares a maximum byte length in its summary as a "(max N bytes)" token; a string exceeding its bound is fatal "invalid_argument". The bound is machine-readable: the code generator extracts it from the summary token, the schema requires every string argument's summary to carry the token, and CI lints that it appears exactly once. A null string (legal only where allow-null is set) and an empty string are encoded identically (length 0) and are treated as equivalent - resource relies on this (null or empty both mean the whole realm).
PETITION EVENT ORDERING. resolved and vitrin_consent.state are sequenced only within their own petition's lifecycle (zero or more state events, then exactly one resolved) and do NOT participate in the cross-request "in request order" rule, because a petition's resolution waits on an unbounded human consent delay. A later sync's done reflects that earlier requests were processed and that any petition among them was registered and its consent initiated; it does NOT wait for that petition to resolve. A blocking client therefore reads resolved on its own schedule without deadlocking against an unrelated pending prompt.

interface.name: vitrin_handshake
interface.description:
The connection-lifecycle object of a principal connection, implicit object 1 at connect: the authentication gate, the fatal-error channel, and the sync barrier. It lives for the whole connection.
Handshake state machine: in the initial state the only legal message is hello. After hello the client MAY pipeline further requests; the server queues them during credential verification and processes them after vitrin_principal.bound is sent (if verification fails the connection dies "auth_failed" and queued requests are never processed). Any traffic before a first hello is fatal "pre_handshake", delivered best-effort if the frame parsed; unparseable garbage may be closed silently. Either way the reason is logged.
The human principal has no wire presence in version 1: host input in nested mode is the implicit human, and only agents handshake.

request.name: hello
request.description:
The only pre-authentication message. Presents a credential to the core's pluggable verifier and pre-allocates the principal object that a successful handshake will bind. Success is announced by vitrin_principal.bound; failure is fatal "auth_failed" or "version_unsupported".
The credential encoding is deliberately opaque to the wire: credential_type names a scheme (for example "static-token", "spiffe-jwt-svid", "oidc", "ssh-cert"; at most 32 bytes) and credential carries scheme-defined bytes (at most 32768 bytes), interpreted only by the verifier. identity is the SPIFFE-shaped identity URI being claimed (at most 2048 bytes, the SPIFFE-ID maximum: a 255-byte trust domain plus path). It is a routing hint; the authoritative principal identity is the verifier-canonical string later delivered in vitrin_principal.bound, never this claimed value. The wire hard-wires no scheme; this is the signature-agility hook for future credential families, and credentials larger than one frame arrive via an fd-borne sibling request in a future version. Sender-constraint is the triple of this connection, the verified credential, and SO_PEERCRED recorded at accept: a handle minted on one connection presented on another is fatal "invalid_object".
The credential is secret material: the server MUST NOT write credential bytes into logs, error.message text, or the flight recorder - at most credential_type and the byte length may be recorded.
hello is legal exactly once per connection: its opcode is defined only in the initial state, so a second hello - during verification or after bound - is fatal "invalid_opcode".
This signature is frozen forever.

arg.name: version
arg.summary: protocol version; version 1 requires exact match

arg.name: identity
arg.summary: claimed identity URI, e.g. vitrin://local/agent/demo (max 2048 bytes)

request.name: sync
request.description: Requests a done event carrying the same cookie. The done event is sent only after every request received before this one has been processed and every event those requests caused has been queued ahead of it - with one exemption: petition-lifecycle events (resolved, vitrin_consent.state) wait on human consent and do not participate in the barrier; done confirms a petition was registered and its consent initiated, never that it resolved (see PETITION EVENT ORDERING). Because actuation requests are fire-and-forget and enforcement failures are events, a threadless blocking client sends its actuations, syncs, then reads until done, raising on any refused event seen - bounding failure discovery to one round trip without per-actuation acknowledgements. Valid only after bound; a cookie echo, not a callback object, so it costs no id churn.

event.name: error

description.summary: fatal protocol error; the connection closes

event.description: The connection-fatal error channel. object_id is the id of the object where the error occurred (which may be 1, this object); code is namespaced by that object's interface error enum - in version 1 the only error enum is on this interface, so all fatal codes are connection-global. message is free-form debugging text and is never machine-parsed. After sending this event the server closes the connection. Delivery is best-effort: backpressure deaths (a peer that stops reading) and unframeable streams are closed without it.

arg.name: object_id
arg.summary: id of the object where the error occurred

arg.name: code
arg.summary: error code, namespaced by the cited object's interface

arg.name: message
arg.summary: free-form debug description, never parsed (max 1024 bytes)

event.name: done
event.description: Answers sync: all requests received before the corresponding sync have been processed and their events queued ahead of this event.

enum.name: error
enum.description: Every condition here is one a correct client can never trigger; the fuzz target (hostile bytes, fd bombs, forged ids) maps every decode failure onto exactly one of these codes with a clean connection death, and error paths always close any received file descriptor.

entry.name: invalid_object
entry.summary: unknown or foreign object id, id reuse at or below the watermark, reserved-range id, or multi-new_id rule violation

entry.name: invalid_opcode
entry.summary: opcode not defined for the interface at the negotiated version, including other-class opcodes and a second hello (hello's opcode is defined only in the initial connection state)

entry.name: invalid_argument
entry.summary: argument decode failure: bad UTF-8, embedded NUL, string over its bound, out-of-range enum value, forbidden control character, zero verbs, malformed padding

entry.name: oversized
entry.summary: declared frame size below the 8-byte header minimum, or a payload shorter than the size declares; the 65535-byte ceiling binds senders (a u16 cannot express more)

entry.name: fd_violation
entry.summary: fd count in the header disagrees with the message signature, or unsolicited fds attached

entry.name: pre_handshake
entry.summary: traffic before a first hello on a principal connection

entry.name: version_unsupported
entry.summary: hello carried a protocol version the server does not implement; downgrade is refusal

entry.name: auth_failed
entry.summary: credential rejected: unknown identity, bad token, verifier failure, or SO_PEERCRED mismatch

entry.name: internal
entry.summary: server-side failure that poisoned the connection

entry.name: resource_exhausted
entry.summary: a documented per-connection resource bound was breached: the petition-rate ceiling, the live-object cap, or object-id exhaustion; denial-of-service confinement, not a semantic judgement

interface.name: vitrin_principal
interface.description: The bound identity: the root of the connection's authority chain, holding exactly the authority to address realms and petition for grants. Pre-allocated by hello and live upon bound. All of the principal's grants die with the connection - version 1 has no grant persistence (restore tokens are a future version's addition).

event.name: bound
event.description: The terminal event of a successful handshake. identity is the canonical identity as normalized and verified by the core's verifier and recorded in the grant table - not an echo of the client's claimed string. Everything the consent prompt and the flight recorder later render about this principal derives from this verifier-owned value, never from free client text.

request.name: get_realm

description.summary: mint an address handle for a realm

request.description: Creates a realm address object for a realm known by name ("realm-0" is the single well-known realm of version 1). Naming is not authority: this request always succeeds structurally, and holding a realm handle only lets the principal petition. A name that is unknown or vacant yields a handle whose petitions resolve "unavailable" - realm absence is a race, not a protocol error, because realms are dynamic in later phases.

interface.name: vitrin_realm
interface.description: An addressing scope for petitions: grants attach to realms, and apps launch into realms. Deliberately authority-free - the handle answers "which realm are you asking about", nothing more. Realm ids are in the protocol from day one so that later multi-realm phases add enumeration and lifecycle events to this interface instead of re-plumbing addressing.

request.name: request_grant

description.summary: petition for authority over this realm

request.description:
Petitions for a grant and mints, in one request, the grant handle, its consent observer, and the three authority facets (view, pointer actuator, text actuator). All five new_id arguments follow the multi-new_id rule (distinct, increasing, above the watermark). The facets are born inert: they confer nothing until the grant resolves granted, and each facet's requests are checked at use time against the grant's effective verb set at the single enforcement chokepoint - a facet whose verb was not granted refuses "not_granted" recoverably. Creation order mirrors attenuation: nothing about this petition is observable through any object the petitioner does not hold.
resource selects what within the realm; null or empty means the whole realm (the only granularity version 1 serves). The string vocabulary is type-prefixed ("surface:...", "node:...") and grows by version without a new request (max 256 bytes). verbs is the requested verb set and MUST be non-zero (an empty petition is fatal "invalid_argument"). expiry_ms of 0 means bounded only by the persistence rung. max_event_rate is in events per second, governs observation and actuation alike, and 0 selects the server's default ceiling - never unlimited. persistence is the requested rung; the durable rungs (until_revoked, always) exist in the enum from day one but resolve "unsupported" in version 1, pending provenance verification in a later phase. Clients MUST send flags 0 in version 1; bit 0 is reserved for the one_shot constraint. flags references no enum and is deliberately not wire-validated, so a set reserved bit is not a protocol error: it resolves "unsupported" - honest refusal rather than accepted-and-unenforced. Future boolean constraints are flags bits; future value-bearing constraints (such as focus conditions) arrive as a since-gated builder request preceding this one.
Version 1 policy: pending-petition admission is capped per verified identity, across all of that identity's connections (not merely per connection - opening many connections under one credential must not multiply concurrent prompts), and the deployment additionally enforces a global ceiling on concurrent-plus-queued prompts. Excess petitions resolve "busy" (the consent-fatigue valve). request_grant is itself subject to a server-side petition-rate ceiling and a per-connection live-object cap; because every petition permanently allocates five object ids (version 1 has no destructors), a connection that breaches either bound - or exhausts the id space itself - is closed fatally "resource_exhausted", confining the denial-of-service to the offending connection rather than the whole core. A pending petition is withdrawn if the connection closes: consent is in-context, so the prompt disappears with the petitioner.

arg.name: view
arg.summary: observation facet (inert until granted with observe)

arg.name: pointer
arg.summary: pointer facet (inert until granted with actuate_pointer)

arg.name: text
arg.summary: text facet (inert until granted with actuate_text)

arg.name: resource
arg.summary: resource selector within the realm; null or empty = whole realm (max 256 bytes)

arg.name: verbs
arg.summary: requested verb set; MUST be non-zero

arg.name: expiry_ms
arg.summary: requested lifetime in milliseconds; 0 = bounded by the persistence rung

arg.name: max_event_rate
arg.summary: requested ceiling in events per second for observation and actuation; 0 = server default, never unlimited

arg.name: flags
arg.summary: boolean constraint bits; MUST be 0 in version 1 (bit 0 reserved: one_shot)

interface.name: vitrin_grant
interface.description:
The wire projection of one grant-table row (principal x resource x verbs x constraints) and the single voice of the enforcement chokepoint: every capture and every actuation under this grant is checked by one server-side function whose refusals are delivered here. Born pending by request_grant, conferring nothing; exactly one resolved event ever decides its fate. A grant that later expires or is revoked goes dead and its facets go inert - their requests refuse recoverably, never fatally.
Version 1 defines no requests on this interface. Documented growth seams for later versions, each purely additive: a release destructor (withdraw a pending petition or relinquish authority early, with the tombstone rule that clients discard events to released ids), an asynchronous revoked push event (resolved still fires exactly once, ever; refused remains the enforcement-bearing signal), attenuation (minting narrower child grants), restore tokens, and an epoch-staleness refusal sibling carrying the current epoch for compare-and-swap actuation.

event.name: resolved
event.description: Sent exactly once per grant, ever: the terminal event of the pending phase, after the consent decision (or policy decision) completes. On outcome granted, the remaining arguments carry the EFFECTIVE authority - the verb set, persistence rung, and expiry the human actually chose, which may be narrower than requested (Allow-once versus Allow-while-running changes the lifetime). On any other outcome the trailing arguments are zero. The effective max_event_rate is deliberately not echoed here: an agent discovers throttling operationally, through refused(rate_limited) and its retry_after_ms hint. Denial and timeout are clean distinct events, never a hang and never a connection death.

arg.name: expiry_ms
arg.summary: effective lifetime in milliseconds; 0 = bounded by the rung

event.name: refused

description.summary: the chokepoint refused one use of this grant

event.description: The single recoverable-error event for grant use, covering capture and actuation alike - one chokepoint, one refusal voice. verb names the verb whose use was refused, which also identifies the facet. For the reply-bearing capture_frame this event is that capture's terminal (exactly one of frame_ready or refused per capture, in request order, never coalesced). For fire-and-forget actuations refusals may be coalesced per the delivery classification. retry_after_ms is greater than zero only for rate_limited and hints when the token bucket refills.

arg.name: verb
arg.summary: the verb whose use was refused

arg.name: retry_after_ms
arg.summary: refill hint in milliseconds; nonzero only for rate_limited

enum.name: verb
enum.description: The verb bitfield. Later phases append entries (key actuation, credential presentation, subtree reads) without touching version-1 bits. The SDK-level dotted names (observe, actuate.pointer, actuate.text) are these bits.

entry.name: observe
entry.summary: capture frames of the granted resource

entry.name: actuate_pointer
entry.summary: inject pointer motion, buttons, and scroll

entry.name: actuate_text
entry.summary: inject Unicode text

enum.name: persistence
enum.description: The full ladder is defined from day one so the wire never changes shape when durable rungs arrive; version 1 accepts only once and while_running, and refuses the durable rungs "unsupported" because they are valid only with verified provenance (a later phase).

entry.name: once
entry.summary: single-use authority

entry.name: while_running
entry.summary: lives while the requesting principal's connection lives

entry.name: until_revoked
entry.summary: durable until explicitly revoked (requires verified provenance; refused in version 1)

entry.name: always
entry.summary: durable and auto-reissued (requires verified provenance; refused in version 1)

enum.name: outcome
enum.description: Petition-time results, each mapping to a distinct typed SDK error (or success). All are recoverable: a denial is an answer, not a protocol violation.

entry.name: granted
entry.summary: authority active; the event carries the effective verbs, rung, and expiry

entry.name: denied
entry.summary: the human said no

entry.name: timed_out
entry.summary: the consent prompt expired unanswered; petitioning again later is legal

entry.name: unavailable
entry.summary: the realm was unknown, vacant, or closed while the petition was pending

entry.name: unsupported
entry.summary: in-range but refused by policy: durable rung without provenance, reserved flag set, unserved resource prefix, or a defined verb this deployment or resource does not serve (an out-of-range verb bit is instead fatal invalid_argument)

entry.name: busy
entry.summary: the pending-petition admission cap for this verified identity (across all of its connections) was reached

enum.name: refusal
enum.description: Emitted by the enforcement chokepoint on every refused capture or actuation. Each code maps to a distinct typed SDK exception: NotGranted, GrantExpired, Revoked, RateLimited, Preempted, ConsentHeld, NoSurface, OperationFailed.

entry.name: not_granted
entry.summary: the grant is not (or not yet) active, or the verb is outside its effective set: use while pending, through an ungranted facet, or after any non-granted resolution (denied, timed_out, unavailable, unsupported, busy)

entry.name: expired
entry.summary: the grant's expiry passed; checked on use and by a proactive timer

entry.name: revoked
entry.summary: revoked by hold-Esc, panel, or policy; effective on the very next request

entry.name: rate_limited
entry.summary: the token bucket is empty; retry_after_ms hints the refill

entry.name: preempted
entry.summary: physical human input owns the target right now

entry.name: consent_held
entry.summary: the principal's own pending petition has a prompt up; that principal's actuation is refused (never delivered to the app) until the prompt closes; other principals' grants are unaffected

entry.name: no_surface
entry.summary: the realm has no surface (its shim crashed or exited); never a stale frame

entry.name: internal
entry.summary: server-side failure during this use (renderer, memfd, delivery)

interface.name: vitrin_consent
interface.description:
The prompt-visibility lifecycle of exactly one petition, visible to exactly its petitioner. Scoping is structural: this object is minted by request_grant itself, so an agent cannot name - and therefore cannot observe - consent activity for any petition it did not make. The interface deliberately carries no requests: nothing an agent sends can put content in front of the human, and everything the prompt renders is core-validated data (the verifier-canonical identity, the parsed verbs, realm, and expiry). The authoritative decision is never here: it arrives as vitrin_grant.resolved, so a blocking client may ignore consent events entirely.
The consent overlay is composited into human-visible output only; it never appears in captured frames - agents cannot watch prompts. Consent decisions are not protocol-expressible by design: the scripted-consent injector used by integration tests is a build-gated core hook, not a wire message.

event.name: state
event.description: Zero or more transitions, all delivered before the grant's resolved event: queued (the prompt waits behind another prompt or a policy decision), shown (the prompt is visible, all physical input now routes exclusively to it, and the agent knows to keep waiting), closed (the prompt is gone; the decision follows on the grant). Under an auto-approve consent policy (headless CI, explicitly flagged and loudly logged) the server may emit only closed, or no transitions at all.

entry.name: queued
entry.summary: waiting behind another prompt or a policy decision

entry.name: shown
entry.summary: visible; physical input is grabbed by the prompt

entry.name: closed
entry.summary: gone; the decision arrives on the grant

interface.name: vitrin_view
interface.description: The observation capability onto a realm's composited framebuffer: in version 1, one view is the realm's whole view. Capture is a poll model: one request, one frame, no streaming. Minted inert by request_grant; every capture passes the enforcement chokepoint (grant alive, observe granted, rate bucket) and refuses recoverably via vitrin_grant.refused when it fails. The agent learns the view's dimensions from frame_ready; version 1 has no geometry protocol.

request.name: capture_frame

description.summary: request one frame of the realm view

request.description: Reply-bearing: exactly one terminal event per request - frame_ready on success or vitrin_grant.refused(observe, ...) on failure - in request order, never coalesced. Pipelining captures is legal; replies pair in order. The pairing is forced by the type system: fd arguments have no null form, so failure must be a distinct event. Captures are rate-limited by the grant's max_event_rate.

event.name: frame_ready
event.description: Exactly one per successful capture_frame. The fd is a fresh memfd containing the frame - always a copy; agents never see live buffers. Ownership of the fd transfers to the receiver, which MUST close it after use (the server closes its own copy after sending). Version 1 pixels are xrgb8888, row-major, origin top-left, little-endian, and stride equals width * 4 exactly - this pins the golden-frame tests and makes observation digests unambiguous (the digest domain is the whole buffer). flags is always 0 in version 1; the reserved bits make a later zero-copy dmabuf handoff this same message with a flag, never a new signature.

arg.name: fd
arg.summary: fresh memfd holding the frame; ownership transfers to the receiver

arg.name: stride
arg.summary: row stride in bytes; equals width * 4 in version 1

enum.name: format
enum.description: Values are DRM fourcc codes so the enum never diverges from the kernel's format namespace when dmabuf arrives. Shared by vitrin_shim_surface.attach.

entry.name: xrgb8888
entry.summary: 32-bit xRGB, DRM_FORMAT_XRGB8888

entry.name: argb8888
entry.summary: 32-bit ARGB, DRM_FORMAT_ARGB8888

entry.name: y_invert
entry.summary: rows are bottom-up (reserved; never set in version 1)

entry.name: dmabuf
entry.summary: fd is a dmabuf, not a memfd (reserved; never set in version 1)

interface.name: vitrin_actuator_pointer
interface.description: The pointer-injection capability: move, button, and scroll, folded into one pointer class for version 1. All coordinates are realm-view pixels - what the agent observed in a captured frame is what it addresses; coordinates outside the view are clamped (detecting that the target moved underneath a stale observation is the epoch mechanism of a later phase). Minted inert by request_grant. All requests are fire-and-forget: failures arrive as vitrin_grant.refused(actuate_pointer, ...), coalescible, bounded by the sync barrier. A client-level click is move, button press, button release, sync. Later versions add intent-level motion (drag with duration and easing, interpolated server-side) as sibling requests; these primitives stay valid forever.

request.name: move
request.description: Moves this principal's virtual pointer to realm-view (x, y).

request.name: button

description.summary: press or release a pointer button

request.description: Presses or releases a button at the current pointer position. Button codes are Linux evdev codes (BTN_LEFT is 0x110).

request.name: scroll
request.description: High-resolution scroll on one axis; one wheel notch is a value120 of plus or minus 120.

entry.name: released
entry.summary: button released

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: button pressed

entry.name: vertical
entry.summary: vertical scroll

entry.name: horizontal
entry.summary: horizontal scroll

interface.name: vitrin_actuator_text
interface.description: The text-injection capability. Semantics are "deliver this Unicode string", never "press these keys": the payload bypasses keymaps and input methods entirely, and the delivery path (the shim's dynamically generated keymap) is an implementation detail the agent cannot observe. Minted inert by request_grant; fire-and-forget, refusals via vitrin_grant.refused(actuate_text, ...). Key chords are deliberately not expressible by agents in version 1 - that is a distinct key actuation verb reserved for a later phase.

request.name: type
request.description: Delivers UTF-8 text of at most 4096 bytes to the granted target. Normative control-character rule: a newline (U+000A) MUST be rendered as a Return keypress and a tab (U+0009) as Tab by the delivery path - this is how an agent submits a form or presses Enter after a URL. All other C0 and C1 control characters are fatal "invalid_argument": a correct client never emits them.

interface.name: vitrin_shim_session
interface.description:
The connection-lifecycle object of a shim connection, implicit object 1. Authentication is structural: the inherited socketpair is the credential, and the realm identity was assigned at fork - this protocol contains no request by which a shim sets, claims, or changes its realm identity. The shim's protocol version is pinned at spawn (the core and its shims are release-paired; there is no shim hello).
Shim connections carry no fatal-error event: a shim that violates the protocol is logged and its connection closed (named log-only conditions: invalid_buffer for geometry or fd-size lies, bad_order for damage or commit against a never-attached surface or an unknown buffer_id, already_initialized for a second get_seat). Socketpair EOF is shim death: the core survives, closes every in-flight buffer fd, and drops the realm's surface - agents' next captures refuse "no_surface". Version 1 has no restart policy.

event.name: configure
event.description: The core's first message on a shim connection, guaranteed to precede the processing of any shim request - the shim performs one synchronous read at startup before serving its private Wayland socket. Carries the realm identity (informational; the shim can never assert it) and the realm-view size the shim advertises to its app via its own output and window-configure machinery (the single-maximized layout). May be re-sent when the view resizes; a version-1 core may letterbox instead, but the message exists so that resize is never a protocol change.

arg.name: realm
arg.summary: realm identity assigned at fork (max 64 bytes)

request.name: create_surface

description.summary: create a surface for the app's content

request.description: Creates a surface through which the shim forwards its app's committed buffers. Version 1 composites realm surfaces with a trivial single-maximized layout, but nothing in the protocol hard-codes exactly one surface per shim.

request.name: get_seat
request.description: Creates the seat through which the core delivers input for this realm. Exactly one seat per session: a second get_seat is the log-and-close condition already_initialized. Because seat events are addressed to this shim-allocated object, input the core routes to the realm before the shim has created its seat has no destination and is dropped; a well-behaved shim calls get_seat during startup, immediately after receiving configure.

interface.name: vitrin_shim_surface
interface.description: The buffer path from shim to core, with Wayland's proven pending-state semantics: attach and damage mutate pending state only; commit atomically latches it. Buffers are identified by shim-chosen cookies (buffer_id) rather than buffer objects; the buffer_done event echoes the cookie to return ownership. On connection death the core closes every fd it holds.

request.name: attach
request.description: Stages a buffer for the next commit. buffer_id is a shim-chosen cookie naming this buffer in later buffer_done events. In version-1 practice kind is shm: a memfd the core copies in at commit. kind dmabuf is the same message - single-plane, linear modifier implied (there is deliberately no modifier argument the core could fail to honor); explicit modifiers and multi-planar formats arrive as a since-gated parameter builder in a later version, one fd per message, so the one-fd rule never becomes a wall. Geometry inconsistent with the fd's actual size, a zero dimension, or a stride overflow is the log-and-close condition invalid_buffer; re-attaching a dmabuf buffer_id that has not yet received buffer_done is bad_order.

request.name: damage
request.description: Adds a buffer-coordinate damage rectangle to pending state. Repeatable; rectangles accumulate as a union until commit and travel per-rectangle on the wire so damage-only updates are verifiable in logs. Damage is a hint - the core may repaint more - and out-of-bounds rectangles are clamped, not fatal.

request.name: commit
request.description: Latches pending attach and damage atomically into the surface's current state. A commit with no new attach re-presents the current buffer with the new damage (a repaint) - legal, not an error. Damage or commit against a surface that has never been attached is the log-and-close condition bad_order.

event.name: frame_done
event.description: The frame-callback relay: sent after a commit's content has been presented (or would have been, headless). At most one outstanding frame_done per commit, FIFO-correlated; the shim fans it out to its app's frame callbacks so the app throttles to the true output cadence. frame_done is per commit and independent of buffer disposition: a commit whose attached buffer failed (buffer_done with a failure status) re-presents the previous content and still receives its frame_done, so the app's pacing loop never stalls on a rejected buffer.

arg.name: time_ms
arg.summary: presentation time in milliseconds, monotonic domain

event.name: buffer_done

description.summary: buffer ownership returns (exactly once per attach)

event.description:
Terminal disposition of one attach, exactly once per attach, in attach order per surface - including an attach superseded by another attach before commit, which is released promptly without being used. Status released means the core (and GPU) are done with the buffer: the shim, and its app, may reuse it - prompt after the copy under version-1 shm copy-in, at GPU-done under dmabuf passthrough (the same message; only the timing regime changes). The failure statuses mean the buffer was not used (the previously committed content remains on screen) and direct the shim to fall back to shm; ownership returns in the same breath. Deliberately not merged with frame_done: buffer reusability and frame pacing are different facts that only coincide under copy-in.
File-descriptor ownership: the core takes ownership of the fd received in attach and closes it before or as it emits this event for that buffer_id (after copying the pixels out under shm, or after importing under dmabuf, or immediately on a failure status). The shim owns its buffer, never the passed fd, once buffer_done arrives. On connection death the core closes every attach fd it still holds.

entry.name: shm
entry.summary: memfd; the core copies pixels in at commit

entry.name: dmabuf
entry.summary: dmabuf; the core imports it zero-copy, single-plane, linear modifier implied

entry.name: released
entry.summary: the buffer was used (or superseded) and may be reused

entry.name: import_failed
entry.summary: dmabuf import failed; fall back to shm; buffer unused and released

entry.name: format_unsupported
entry.summary: format not usable by the renderer; fall back to shm; buffer unused and released

entry.name: too_large
entry.summary: buffer exceeds the renderer's limits; fall back to shm; buffer unused and released

interface.name: vitrin_shim_seat

description.summary: input delivery to the shim (events only, origin-tagged)

interface.description:
Input delivery from core to shim. The shim replays these events to its app through its own virtual seat; the core owns the mapping from principals to shim seats. Every event carries origin as its final argument - per-event tagging, never modal start/stop envelopes (modal state desyncs and fuzzes badly) - preserving the physical-versus-emulated distinction end to end from day one, because physically-originated consent in a later phase is built on it. This structural rule is enforced by the schema.
Pointer coordinates are realm-view pixels; the shim maps view to surface-local coordinates. Focus in version 1 is synthesized shim-side (a single-surface realm: pointer enter on first motion, keyboard focus held on the app); an explicit tagged focus event is the multi-surface addition of a later version.

event.name: motion
event.description: Pointer motion to realm-view (x, y). Coordinates are fixed-point so that later server-side motion synthesis can be sub-pixel without a signature change (the agent-facing move request stays integer because agents address captured pixels).

event.name: button
event.description: Button press or release at the current pointer position; Linux evdev button codes.

event.name: scroll
event.description: High-resolution scroll; one wheel notch is plus or minus 120.

event.name: key
event.description:
A key event for the human path: physical typing in nested mode flows core to shim to app, and humans press chords, arrows, and function keys that a text string cannot carry. Keys travel as xkbcommon keysyms, not keycodes: layout-independent, requiring no keymap-relay message and no keymap interpretation inside the core (nested host input already arrives interpreted), and the shim maps keysyms into the same dynamically generated keymap machinery that text delivery already requires.
Normative modifier-suppression rule: keysyms arrive already modifier-resolved. The shim MUST bind each non-modifier keysym at an unmodified (plain) level of its dynamic keymap for replay, so that modifiers already applied are never applied twice. Modifier keysyms (Shift_L, Control_L, Alt_L, Super_L, and friends) are forwarded as ordinary key events and convey chord state to the app only; they MUST NOT change the level at which subsequent resolved keysyms bind. Documented version-1 limitation: raw-scancode fidelity for keymap-sensitive apps is a later version's keymap relay plus keycode event.

event.name: text
event.description: Text delivery - the agent actuation path in version 1, always origin emulated. The shim renders the string via its dynamic keymap; a newline MUST be rendered as Return and a tab as Tab, mirroring the actuator contract. The origin tag on text is what keeps a later phase's human input-method text (origin physical) purely additive.

entry.name: released
entry.summary: key released

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: key pressed

enum.name: origin
enum.description: The libei/EIS distinction, preserved through the hop where libei drops it: physical means a real human input device produced this event; emulated means a principal's actuator (or, later, motion synthesis) produced it. Present on every seat event as the final argument, from day one, because later phases hang physically-originated consent on it.

entry.name: physical
entry.summary: produced by a physical human input device

entry.name: emulated
entry.summary: produced by a principal's actuator
